pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Something deletes one of your pods. Walk me through what happens until the container is gone — and tell me which two things happen at the same time.
expected_points: the API server sets a deletionTimestamp and the terminationGracePeriodSeconds clock starts
in parallel: the endpoints controller removes the pod from the Service's EndpointSlice and every kube-proxy/ingress has to catch up, while the kubelet runs preStop and then sends SIGTERM to PID 1
nothing synchronises those two chains
when the grace period expires the kubelet sends SIGKILL, which cannot be caught or handled

questions.prompt: Which has to happen first: the pod leaving the Service's endpoints, or your server refusing new connections? What breaks in the other order, and what does the caller actually see?
expected_points: endpoint removal first — the pod must stop being a routing target before it stops accepting
otherwise kube-proxy still forwards new connections to a closed listener
the caller gets connection refused or a reset, not an HTTP status, on a request that was never served
two levers: fail readiness immediately (for anything that polls it) and a preStop sleep to delay SIGTERM (for the deletion race)

questions.prompt: Show me the shutdown path in your Go service. Why Shutdown and not Close, why the timeout, and why isn't ErrServerClosed an error?
expected_points: signal.NotifyContext turns SIGTERM/SIGINT into a cancelled context
flip readiness to false first, then call srv.Shutdown
Close severs in-flight requests; Shutdown closes listeners and idle connections and waits for active ones
the shutdown context needs a deadline below the grace period so one stuck handler cannot burn the whole budget
Serve returns http.ErrServerClosed on a clean stop; reporting it exits non-zero and makes a normal deploy look like a crash

questions.prompt: preStop sleeps 10s, SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT is 20s, terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 25. What happens, and when?
expected_points: the preStop hook runs inside the grace period, not before it — the clock starts at deletion
SIGTERM arrives at ~10s, leaving only ~15s of drain
at 25s the kubelet sends SIGKILL and cuts the drain short: dropped connections and no shutdown log
the fix is preStop + shutdown timeout + margin <= terminationGracePeriodSeconds

questions.prompt: Why does your service have both /healthz and /readyz when they look identical? What must each one never check?
expected_points: readiness answers 'should I get new requests' and is 503 for the whole drain, which is how the pod leaves the endpoints
liveness answers 'is this process wedged' and must keep returning 200 throughout the drain
a liveness probe pointed at the readiness path restarts the container mid-drain
liveness must not check dependencies: a database blip becomes a cluster-wide restart storm, and a restart cannot fix someone else's outage

questions.prompt: Your pod has limits.cpu: 1 on a 64-core node and no GOMAXPROCS. What does the Go runtime do, what does that cost you, and how do you fix it?
expected_points: through Go 1.24 the runtime sizes GOMAXPROCS from the CPU affinity mask — the node's cores — and cannot see the cgroup quota
64 Ps and roughly 25% of them as GC mark workers burn the quota early, the kernel throttles the whole process, tail latency grows
Go 1.25 made the default container-aware on Linux, but it is gated on the module's go directive
fix: set GOMAXPROCS from limits.cpu (literal or downward API resourceFieldRef), or import automaxprocs

questions.prompt: What is GOMEMLIMIT for, why must it sit below limits.memory, and what is wrong with the value "512Mi"?
expected_points: the GC's default target is a ratio of the live heap and knows nothing about the cgroup limit, so the heap can grow until the kernel OOM-kills the process (exit 137, no shutdown)
GOMEMLIMIT is a soft limit the GC aims at; the cgroup limit is hard, so the soft one has to be lower
headroom covers what GOMEMLIMIT excludes: the binary's mappings and OS-side memory — 80-90% of the limit is typical
512Mi is Kubernetes syntax; Go wants B/KiB/MiB/GiB/TiB, and an unparseable value stops the runtime from starting

questions.prompt: Explain how maxSurge and maxUnavailable produce a rollout with no failed requests — and how you would prove it rather than assume it.
expected_points: maxUnavailable: 0 means capacity is never removed before a replacement is ready; maxSurge pays for the extra pod
readiness is the gate that decides 'ready', so the rollout is only as good as the readiness probe
each old pod then goes through the same termination sequence, so drain correctness matters as much as the strategy
prove it with a request loop against the Service during the rollout and watch for anything that is not 200; maxSurge 0 with maxUnavailable 0 deadlocks

questions.prompt: You change a value in the ConfigMap. What happens to the running pods, and why is that the behaviour you picked?
expected_points: env vars from envFrom are snapshotted at container creation, so running pods keep the old values
you roll the Deployment, which produces new pods and a revision you can roll back
mounted config would update in place instead — restart-to-change is the trade-off chosen here
logs stay on stdout as structured slog lines because that is the only logging interface the platform reads
